prompt:
A finished graphic design poster, seen flat-on and full bleed; the image is the poster itself, not a mockup on a wall. Printed in flat solid inks on uncoated off-white paper: signal red, sun yellow and black, plus one black-and-white halftone photograph. No gradients, no glow, no gloss, no bevels, no soft shadows; depth only from hard-edged solid shadow planes.

The whole poster is the side of a tram car seen dead flat in side elevation, cropped so the car's body runs off both the left and right edges of the paper. The top third of the sheet is solid black: the night sky, with one straight thin black-and-yellow overhead wire crossing it edge to edge. The tram body below is a flat slab of signal red, with a single sun yellow stripe of one fixed width running along its lower edge from edge to edge, and two plain black wheels half cropped at the bottom edge.

Cut straight through the red tram side, where its windows would be, are four enormous capital letters spelling "HOME", in a heavy bold condensed sans-serif, each letter the size and position of one tram window, side by side, filling the width. The letters are hard-edged windows cut out of the red: inside every letter shape you see a black-and-white halftone photograph, with coarse visible halftone dots, of the interior of a Czech Tatra T3 tram car at night: rows of empty plastic seats, vertical grab poles and hanging strap handles, lit by its own ceiling lights. The photograph shows only inside the letter shapes; the cut edges are razor sharp, no feathering, no blending, no glow at the cut. The letter "O" has a hard black shadow plane on its inner right edge to show the thickness of the tram wall.

Below the tram, on the off-white paper strip at the very bottom, in heavy black capitals, the words "NEW NIGHT TRAM". Between the window letters and the yellow stripe, smaller, in sun yellow capitals on the red, the words "ALL NIGHT".

Flat even light on the graphic parts; the photograph is lit only from inside the tram. The only words on the poster are exactly "HOME", "ALL NIGHT" and "NEW NIGHT TRAM". No other text, no small print, no logos, no route numbers, no placeholder text, no people in the photograph, no moon, no stars, no stock-photo finish.

A finished graphic design poster, seen flat-on and full bleed; the image is the poster itself, not a mockup on a wall. Printed in flat solid inks: a sun yellow ground, with black, cobalt blue and signal red as the working inks, four inks at most. No gradients, no glow, no gloss, no bevels, no soft shadows; depth only from hard-edged solid shadow planes.

The drawing is a strict flat side elevation of a tram street's overhead line. Two tall black steel poles stand at the far left and far right edges of the poster, both cropped by the top and bottom edges. Between them, black overhead wires of one fixed width cross the sheet horizontally, edge to edge, at four heights, like the lines of a stave. Hanging from these wires, as if they were heavy street signs bolted to the catenary, are four rows of enormous bold heavy sans-serif capital letters, one word per wire, reading top to bottom: "THE", "WIRE", "STAYS", "ON". Each letter is a solid cobalt blue block with a thick hard black extruded shadow down and to the right, so the letters read as heavy hanging slabs; each word hangs by short black hangers from its wire. The words are so large that they fill almost the whole width, leaving very little empty yellow.

At the bottom of the poster, a small tram drawn flat in side elevation from simple rectangles, signal red body, black windows, runs along a black ground line that exits both edges. Its black diamond-shaped pantograph rises and touches the underside of the word "ON", and at the touching point is one single small hard-edged spark drawn as a flat white eight-pointed zigzag star, no glow around it. The tram is small, under one-sixth of the poster height, so the hanging words dwarf it. The tram's front end runs off the right edge of the paper, breaking the frame.

On the side of the tram, in sun yellow capitals, the words "NIGHT LINE".

Flat even light, no light source; the yellow ground stands for the light of the street lamps. The only words on the poster are exactly "THE WIRE STAYS ON" and "NIGHT LINE". No other text, no small print, no logos, no placeholder text, no moon, no stars, no skyline, no lightning bolts, no glow.

A finished graphic design poster, seen flat-on and full bleed; the image is the poster itself, not a mockup on a wall. Printed in flat solid inks on uncoated off-white paper, three inks only: signal red, cobalt blue and black. No gradients, no glow, no gloss, no bevels, no soft shadows; depth only from hard-edged solid shadow planes.

The poster is built from one massive block of lettering. The words "LAST TRAM" are stacked on two lines in enormous bold heavy condensed sans-serif capitals, cobalt blue, filling almost the whole width of the sheet, with a continuous solid black extruded shadow running down and to the left from every letter so the two words fuse into a single heavy monolith, like a concrete platform. The word "LAST" is on top, "TRAM" below it, both tightly kerned so the letters touch.

A single signal-red transit-map line of one fixed thick width enters from the top-left edge of the paper, bends at a clean 45 degree corner, and runs straight horizontally through the middle of the word "LAST", striking it out like a crossing-out stroke; along this stretch sit four round station dots, white with thick black rings, one on each letter of "LAST". The red line then bends at 90 degrees with the same corner radius, drops down past the right side of "TRAM", and runs off the bottom-right edge of the paper, breaking out of the frame. Above the struck-out word, small but heavy, the single word "NO" in black capitals sits at the first station like a station name.

Below the monolith, the line "NEW NIGHT LINE" in bold black capitals, set along the red route's lower stretch as its station label. The off-white paper fills the remaining space; the lettering block is big enough that there is little empty field.

Flat even light, no light source. Transit-map lines of one fixed width with black-ringed station dots, bending only at 45 and 90 degrees with one corner radius; the line starts at the paper edge and ends at the paper edge. Bold heavy sans-serif lettering; the only words on the poster are exactly "NO", "LAST TRAM" and "NEW NIGHT LINE". No other text, no small print, no logos, no placeholder text, no clocks, no moon, no stars, no drawing of a tram.

A finished graphic design poster, seen flat-on and full bleed; the image is the poster itself, not a mockup on a wall. Printed in flat solid inks: cobalt blue, black, sun yellow and signal red, four inks at most, no paper showing. No gradients, no glow, no gloss, no bevels, no soft shadows; depth only from hard-edged solid shadow planes.

True isometric drawing at 30 degrees: verticals stay vertical, parallel edges stay parallel, no vanishing point. The whole poster, edge to edge, is a dense isometric city grid seen from above: rows of plain rectangular city blocks of varied heights, packed tight, running off all four edges of the sheet. Every block has cobalt blue top faces, black left faces and black right faces: a sleeping city at night, all hard flat planes, no texture.

Two of the blocks, the biggest and most central, are built out of lettering: the word "STILL" and below it the word "RUNNING", in enormous bold heavy sans-serif capitals extruded up into solid isometric buildings, standing in the grid like the other blocks, with their letter-tops in signal red and their side faces in black. The lettering is lined up with the isometric axes, the letter faces skewed exactly onto the grid. These two lettered blocks are the largest mass on the poster and must read at a glance.

Through the streets between the blocks runs one single sun yellow tram line of one fixed width, entering from the bottom-left edge of the poster, following the isometric streets, turning only at the grid's corners with one consistent corner radius, passing in front of and between the letters of "STILL RUNNING", and leaving by the top-right edge. Along the yellow line sit five black-ringed white station dots. On each block that the yellow line passes, exactly one small square window is sun yellow; every other window in the city is dark.

Flat even night light: the darkness is the cobalt and black planes themselves. The only words on the poster are exactly "STILL RUNNING". No other text, no small print, no logos, no placeholder text, no moon, no stars, no skyline silhouette, no rounded clay blocks, no pastel colours, no three-point perspective.

A finished graphic design poster, seen flat-on and full bleed; the image is the poster itself, not a mockup on a wall. Printed in flat solid inks: black, cobalt blue, sun yellow and signal red, four inks at most. No gradients, no glow, no gloss, no bevels, no soft shadows; depth only from hard-edged solid shadow planes.

The whole poster is the side of a tram at a stop, at night, seen dead flat in elevation and cropped close, so the tram's cobalt blue body fills the sheet and runs off the left, right and top edges. In the middle of it is a pair of tall double doors, opening outward. The left door leaf is the word "STEP" and the right door leaf is the word "IN": each word is set in enormous bold heavy condensed sans-serif capitals, signal red, stacked vertically letter above letter so that each word is as tall as a door and the letters themselves form the door panels. Each door leaf has a hard flat black shadow plane on its inner edge, showing it is swinging open.

Between the two opening leaves is a tall vertical gap of flat solid sun yellow: the light from inside the tram. This yellow shape spills down out of the door, over a black step plate, and falls onto the black pavement at the bottom of the poster as a hard-edged yellow trapezoid of light that runs off the bottom edge of the paper, breaking the frame. Standing on the edge of the yellow light, about to step in, is one tiny figure built from simple geometric shapes, a black rectangle coat and a red circle head, under one-tenth of the poster height, to show how big the doors are.

Above the doors, on the cobalt blue tram body, a black destination band carries the words "NIGHT TRAM" in sun yellow capitals.

Flat even light: the only light is the yellow plane itself, with no glow at its edges. The only words on the poster are exactly "STEP", "IN" and "NIGHT TRAM". No other text, no small print, no logos, no route numbers, no placeholder text, no moon, no stars, no glass reflections, no Corporate Memphis people.

A finished graphic design poster, seen flat-on and full bleed; the image is the poster itself, not a mockup on a wall. Printed in flat solid inks: an ultramarine blue ground, with sun yellow, signal red and black as the working inks, four inks at most. No gradients, no glow, no gloss, no bevels, no soft shadows; depth only from hard-edged solid shadow planes.

True isometric drawing at 30 degrees: verticals stay vertical, parallel edges stay parallel, no vanishing point. In the centre-left of the poster rises a tall narrow isometric tower made of stacked rectangular floors, like a timetable turned into a building. Each floor is a slab block whose front-left face carries a huge two-digit number in heavy bold sans-serif, skewed exactly onto the face: the floors alternate "00" and "30", "00" and "30", going up, ten floors in all. The "00" floors are sun yellow with black numerals, the "30" floors are signal red with sun yellow numerals; every right-hand side face of the tower is solid black, a hard shadow plane. The tower is so tall that its top floors run straight off the top edge of the poster, cropped, breaking the frame.

At the foot of the tower, on a flat isometric street slab, a small boxy tram is drawn in the same strict isometric, built from simple rectangles: sun yellow body, black windows, a single thin black pantograph on its roof touching a straight black overhead wire that runs from the tram off the left edge of the poster. The tram is small, under one-sixth of the image height, to show how tall the timetable is.

To the right of the tower, running vertically up the right side of the ultramarine ground and reading from bottom to top, the headline "EVERY HALF HOUR" in very large bold heavy sans-serif capitals, sun yellow, set tight so it fills the whole height of the right side and leaves almost no empty blue. At the base, skewed onto the top face of the street slab in black capitals, the words "NIGHT TRAM".

Flat even night light with no light source: the darkness is the ultramarine ground itself. The only words on the poster are exactly "EVERY HALF HOUR", "NIGHT TRAM" and the numerals "00" and "30". No other text, no small print, no logos, no placeholder text, no clock faces, no moon, no stars, no rounded clay shapes, no pastel colours.
